Third, he composed the *Treatise on the Teaching of Identity*, refuting the errors of the preceding two [positions] and establishing a single "Teaching of Identity.

Consequently, false doctrines arose, with practitioners resorting to deceitful sophistry that misled later followers; erroneous practices became deeply entrenched, and those unacquainted with the sūtras and śāstras failed to perceive the original source.

Truly, it is now a matter of nothing but arms and weapons, increasing strife and contention. Turning one's back on the Buddhas and Patriarchs, one clings dogmatically to a single lineage of transmission.

Though one may brandish a solitary blade and shout with high voice, the masses jeer and refuse to join in harmony. One must lament the degeneracy of the times and sigh that the True Dharma is gradually sinking away.

I have thus expounded the *Yunhua Ronghui Zhang* (Chapter on the Merging of Cloud-Flowers), hoping thereby to facilitate understanding of the *Xianshou Fenqiji* (Record of the Distinctions of the Master of the First Principle).

As the incense burns and transforms, I cast it into the ocean of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā-samudra*). With focused resolve, I offer this prayer: may the Holy Mind bestow its grace upon those who investigate the profound mysteries so that they may awaken to their original mind;
and may those of penetrating knowledge be free from partiality and bias, clarifying correct insight and vision, and thereby fulfilling their vow to repay the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
En. In the seventh year of the Qiandao era, while sitting out the summer retreat at Yucen, I read this chapter of the teachings and have recorded these notes for my own reference.
Now, the "Chapter on the Harmonization of Meanings" is divided into two sections: first, the explanation of the general title; second, the interpretation of the main text.
First, regarding the explanation of the title: the subsequent title identifies the author. The title reads: "The Meaning of the Harmonization of the One Vehicle and the Forty Unimpeded Eloquences."
"Later, [the text] explains and harmonizes the three vehicles, decisively revealing the wondrous intent of the One Vehicle.
*Commentary:* The first five characters constitute the title; the subsequent eight characters point to the text to explain its meaning.

They refer to the teaching on unimpeded eloquence (*anāvaraṇa-pratibhāna*) in the ninth stage (*bhūmi*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, as is clearly evident in the subsequent scriptural passages. Thus, Master Xianshou said: "In this stage, one performs the Great Dharma..."
The Master clarifies the ritual procedures for expounding the Dharma; therefore, he reveals the distinctions in the textual meaning between the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) and the Three Vehicles (Triyāna).
Next, the twelve characters provide a concise explanation of their harmonious integration. "Fusion" (yōng) means to harmonize; "convergence" (huì) means to take up and unify.

Taking the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of the essence of the One Vehicle as that which performs the fusion and convergence, and taking the teachings and meanings of the Three Vehicles—which flow from it—as the objects [of that fusion and convergence].

This is what Master Rong has realized. It is the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Great Sage to guide and gather those of the three vehicles (*triyāna*), causing them to realize the original source and decisively reveal the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), thereby knowing the wondrous true interest. Therefore, Qingliang, in his commentary on that sutra, said:
"The three vehicles are harmonized to return together to the single reality, for within the mark of liberation there is no differentiation. Next, the person who recorded this is Li...
Composed by Śramaṇa Zhinan of Zhixiang Monastery on Mount Zhongnan during the Tang Dynasty. He was the fourth patriarch of the Huayan school.
The name of the mountain, the designation of the monastery, and the details of his patriarchal conduct and lineage are fully recorded in his biographies.

△ Second, the explanation of the main text. Following the structural outline of the sutra, the major sections are divided into three: first, the introductory section explaining the causes and conditions;

second, the main section clarifying the commonalities and differences; third, the concluding section for circulation that points to the extensive teachings. Furthermore, within the first section, the introductory explanation of the causes and conditions, there are seven parts.
First, the praise of virtues wherein the fundamental principle is shown to encompass both commonalities and differences.

The chapter states: Now, the Dharma of Perfect Penetration takes the possession of virtue as its primary principle. It is realized through the two gates of the principle of dependent origination and practical application.
These two gates refer to what are known as the Common and Distinct Teachings.
The commentary states: The term "Now" (*fu*) marks the beginning of speech and the commencement of praising the Dharma.

It is an exclamation of the inconceivable wondrous virtue of the *Avataṃsaka*’s perfect, penetrating ocean of nature, which takes the fundamental essence and its function as its basis and whose dependent origination is boundless. In truth, principle and phenomena are fused, and the one and the three are unimpeded;

the capacities of beings open to both the root and the branches, and the teachings encompass both the universal and the particular. A single dharma universally subsumes all, and the two gates are brought into accord. (2)
"Gate" refers to the gates of the two teachings: the Shared and the Distinct. △ Second, listing the Shared and Distinct [teachings] while each opens into root and branch.
First, regarding the Distinct Teaching's root and branch, there are further two parts. First, the heading: "The root is distinct; the branches are shared."
The chapter says: "The Distinct Teaching (biejiao) is distinct from the Three Vehicles.
The commentary explains: "Distinct" carries the meaning of being utterly different. It designates the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* as the fundamental school of the One Vehicle (ekayāna).

This is the vast, primordially inherent wisdom of all Buddhas and sentient beings, which fully possesses the teachings and meanings, as well as the principles and phenomena, the objects and wisdom, and the practices.
The stages, causes, and fruits; the basis, arising, substance, and function; the persons and dharmas, the inverse and the conforming;

and the ten categories of meaning such as response and resonance—each of these possesses ten aspects, and these tens are inexhaustible. They serve as the foundation for all teachings. The fundamental dharma is perfectly interfused, fully encompassing its derivative companions.
The fundamental source of the One Vehicle Dharma is distinct and inexhaustible in its various manifestations.

It is utterly different from the various scriptures concerning the retinues throughout the [Buddha’s] lifetime, as well as the teachings of the Small Vehicle and the Three Vehicles—the provisional doctrines that explain the partial, the perfect, the sudden, the gradual, the expedient, and the real.

Although these ten categories of dharma-gates flow from the source, their manifestation at the end is itself perfect. This single, isolated gate of one mark is called the "teaching of expedient means" and is also termed the "teaching of commonality."
It is also called the "Final Teaching" (mòjiào). In the *Wǔjiàoxiāngshèróngtōng* (Harmonization and Integration of the Five Teachings), Xuánxiù states:
"First, they may be taken collectively as one, meaning that the fundamental and the derivative are fused into a single Great Skillful Dharma. Second, they may be divided into two:

first, the Fundamental Teaching, which refers to the Separate Vehicle of the One Vehicle (*biéjiào yīshēng*), as it is the foundation of all teachings; second, the Derivative Teachings, which refer to the Small Vehicle and the Three Vehicles."

Because it flows from that [source], it is also called the "Ultimate" and the "Expedient Means. When the Three Vehicles and the Lesser Vehicle are viewed in relation to the One Vehicle, they are all considered expedient means;
therefore, the *Jiaozhang* (Treatise on the Teachings) specifically establishes the "Gate of Distinguishing Characteristics" (*fenxiang men*) at its outset.

This reveals that the Separate Teaching of the One Vehicle is the root, while the remaining Three Vehicles are the branches. It enumerates ten distinctions, and regarding the final general distinction, it says: "As for..."

The characteristics of the practices, stages, causes, and fruits elucidated in the Separate Teaching of the One Vehicle (biejiao yisheng) are entirely distinct and different from the established limits of the Three Vehicle teachings;
these are detailed in the sūtras, but a brief summary is as discussed below. Next, the "Gate of Comprehensive Inclusion" (gaishen men) is established.
This reveals the seamless fusion of the Dharma, wherein the branches are identical to the root. All three vehicles are, from the very beginning, entirely the One Vehicle.
There are two reasons for this integration, as detailed in that chapter. The Sixth Patriarch, Qingliang, followed and employed these two approaches.

However, changing "partial exclusion" (*quánjiǎn*) to "total exclusion" and "comprehensive inclusion" (*quánshōu*) to "total inclusion," and further regarding the seamless integration of persons and dharmas as profound, vast, and unobstructed, they are all categorized under the Perfect Teaching (*yuánjiào*).

The Seventh Patriarch Guishan also said: "In the *Xuántán* of the Great Commentary, 'total exclusion' of the various schools refers to the meaning of the nature-arising (*xìngqǐ*) of the Separate Teaching;
'total inclusion' of the various schools refers to the meaning of the dependent origination (*yuánqǐ*) of the Common Teaching."

Nevertheless, because they are distinguished according to the capacities of sentient beings and the nature of the Dharma, two gates are opened. Since persons and dharmas are mutually pervasive, these two gates also penetrate one another;
the non-duality of the two gates constitutes the Huayan Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*), which is the principle of how the true realm gives rise to the myriad phenomena.
Now, it is said that Guishan treats "total inclusion" as the "identical teaching" (*tongjiao*), [extending] from dependent origination up to the Huayan...

In this teaching, the Great Dharma-realm Dependent Origination (*dharmadhātu-pratītyasamutpāda*) is itself the Arising of Nature (*xingqi*). Since conditions and nature mutually give rise to one another, all are inconceivable.

This precisely reveals that within the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), the meanings of being complete, pervasive, and identical are fully present—the same as the ten kinds of inexhaustibility. Therefore, the Fourth Patriarch said:
Furthermore, there is the "sameness of the One Vehicle" (*ekayāna-samatā*). This manifests sameness by contrast with wisdom;

if one draws in the capacities of beings to realize this sameness, then each instance of sameness possesses ten aspects, thereby exhausting the inexhaustible. It is further said that within the sameness and difference [of the vehicles], there is also sameness and difference: that many are identical to one is their sameness.
As for the reconciliation of the two masters, it shall be debated as explained below. The above constitutes the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh [sections].

The four great patriarchs, in their succession of teacher and disciple, have all employed the two gates of "differentiated characteristics" and "comprehensive inclusion" to fully manifest the fundamental dharma and fundamental teaching of the *Avataṃsaka*.
These are taught suddenly and perfectly, corresponding to the nature of reality in both its beginning and end, with each aspect being utterly distinct.
Therefore, the tenth gate of definitive discernment states: "There may be sentient beings who, having fulfilled their understanding and practice regarding the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle,"

Regarding those who realize and enter the ocean of fruition: they perceive that all the aforementioned teachings are, in their entirety, the inexhaustible ocean of nature (*dharmatā-samudra*), formed according to conditions and devoid of any other distinct entities.
Therefore, in his "Establishment of the Teachings," Xianshou distinguishes three schools based on the vehicle of the Dharma (*yāna-dharma*).
He differentiates between the fundamental and the derivative, stating: "The first [school] consists of the two vehicles of the ignorant; the last [school] is the distinct teaching (*pṛthag-deśanā*)."

Regarding the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*): although the three intermediate [teachings]—the Sudden, the Final, and the Initial—differ in their provisional and real aspects, they are collectively categorized as the "Three Vehicles" (*triyāna*) teachings, as they are all equally attained by the three types of persons.

Thus, one should know that the first four teachings are all "provisional" (*anta*) teachings, while the final one—the Perfect—is the "fundamental" (*mūla*) teaching. Nevertheless, although the two intermediate teachings—the Final and the Sudden—are progressively...

Profound and supreme, they discuss the single nature and single characteristic; yet, because of their formal opposition, "one" is also termed "three. Thus, the *Mysterious Text* of the Sixth Patriarch says:

"Although the two teachings—the third and the fourth—eliminate duality and differ from the former, they manifest 'one' through formal opposition, skillfully and expediently according to the capacities of beings.
Therefore, the *Exegesis* (*Yanyi*) explains: "The third is the Final Teaching (*zhongjiao*), and the fourth is the Sudden Teaching (*dunjiao*). These two—"
The Teaching fully elucidates the One Vehicle; thus it is called "merging the two," which differs from the preceding Initial Teaching that maintains the Three Vehicles.
As for the word "although": although it elucidates the One Vehicle, because it does so in contrast to the Three, it is the same as the previous two [teachings] in its numerical reduction.
Thus, the first four [teachings] are all winding and retracted, whereas the final teaching alone is the level path and the foundation of all teachings.
It is further said: "The four are the foundation of the teachings" means that without the ocean there would be no hidden current, and without the root there would be no branches.
Desiring to gradually apply the secondary teachings according to the capacities of beings, one first reveals the fundamental dharma, such as by suddenly expounding this sutra.

Thus we know that the Ultimate One Vehicle is the teaching that accords with the fundamental nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); it distinguishes itself from the preceding four teachings, wherein the three vehicles are all considered derivative or secondary teachings.
Therefore, the topical outline states: "The fundamental is indicated and the derivative is distinguished. △ Second, pointing to the sūtra to conclude the section.
The chapter states: "Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* says that outside the three realms, one separately seeks the Great Ox-Cart.

The commentary explains: This is because the *Lotus Sūtra* finally reveals and clarifies [the truth]. Although it belongs to a different time and place, it serves as a skillful means (*upāya*) for the original teaching.

Accordingly, it adapts to capacities through various concessions, destroying the three [vehicles] to reveal the one, and unifying differences to return to identity. It brings those [beings] together...

This refers to those of indeterminate capacity among the three vehicles who exist simultaneously in different locations. That which is "converged" (*hui*) is the *Lotus Sūtra*’s provisional means of the One Vehicle;

that which is "converged upon" (*sui-hui*) is the three vehicles of initial expedient means and ultimate reality. It only converges those of gradual capacity, refining them until they are matured, so that they may enter the One from the gradual.
Thus, they obtain the great ox-cart apart from the [ordinary] realms, returning to the single Buddha-wisdom. Return.
The Buddha-wisdom of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is precisely the return to the Buddha-wisdom of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. Therefore, Qingliang said:

"The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* subsumes all sutras and returns them to the *Avataṃsaka*, for by means of the particular it encompasses the universal; both are subsumed within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). He further stated:

"While the two sutras differ in their modes of transformation (*huayi*), they are no different in their transformative dharma (*huafa*). Now, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* shares its fundamental dharma with the source, while its mode of transformation subsumes the derivative. This refers to the fundamental [Avataṃsaka].

The branches and the root reflect one another; their flourishing and their subduing mutually support one another. Only when this constitutes the skillful means for gathering in living beings can it be said that the branches are gathered back into the root.

If this is so, why did Qingliang, in his *Discourse on Contradictions*, not accept Tang Ji-zang’s judgment that the *Lotus Sūtra* is a wheel of Dharma for gathering the branches back into the root? Answer: He did not accept Ji-zang because the latter relied entirely upon...
This is the error of confusing the modes of transformation (*huayi*). According to the Dharma, there are only the Great and Small Vehicles;

this is the same as the previous Master Chen’s error of conflating the Sudden and Gradual (*banman*), which results in a failure to distinguish the specific characteristics of the sutras and leads to the stagnation of the Small Vehicle. Thus, the *Yanyi* (Exegesis of Meaning) explains that contradiction, saying: "The position established by this master relies solely on the modes of transformation;

according to the Dharma, there are only the Great and Small Vehicles, which is the same as the previous [view] regarding the Sudden and Gradual. This too is insufficient in its inclusion of the meaning. It further says:
From this point on, those who established these teachings failed to grasp the true meaning of the *Lotus Sūtra* and instead created a separate category for those who were mired in the Lesser Vehicle.
Thus we know that although Jizang judged his teaching to be a "Dharma wheel that gathers the branches back to the root," it nonetheless possessed the three aforementioned faults.
The summary of the meaning is insufficient. According to the judgment of our own school, the words are the same but the meanings differ.

Here, the *Lotus Sūtra* is treated in terms of the method of transformation (*vyavahāra*), while the *Avataṃsaka* is taken as the fundamental dharma (*dharmamūla*). Thus, Qingliang said: "Within the single Buddha-vehicle, he speaks of immeasurable vehicles.
Therefore, that sūtra states: "By the power of skillful means, the Buddhas distinguish and speak [of various vehicles] within the single Buddha-vehicle."
Third: It further states, "Since my attainment of Buddhahood, I have used various causes and conditions, various parables, and immeasurable skillful means to guide sentient beings.

This refers to the flow from the source to the branches. In terms of the ritual of transformation (*saṃdarśana-vidhi*), it is the final revelation that shatters the Small Vehicle to manifest the Great Vehicle, and unifies the three vehicles into one. Thus, Qingliang said: "Though there are many [teachings], they are all subsumed within this."

In the end, they return to the source. Thus, that sutra says: "By means of immeasurable and innumerable skillful expedients (*upāya*), I expound all dharmas solely for the sake of the One Buddha Vehicle.
It further says: "The path you practice is the bodhisattva path," and again: "Ultimately, one reaches the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). Therefore, all are causes for Buddhahood.
Thus, we know that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, relying on the reality, reveals the provisional. This is the teaching.
The one is many; when the provisional is realized, it returns to the real. The many are said to be the one;

therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra*’s skillful means of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) serves as the root that subsumes all branches. Furthermore, the Fourth Patriarch’s *Treatise on the Meaning of the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles* states:

"Moreover, regarding the meaning of the One Vehicle, there are two distinctions: first, the 'True Vehicle' (*bhūtayāna*), as explained in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; second, the 'Provisional Vehicle' (*prajñaptiyāna*)."
It is thus categorized into ten pairs. The first seven pairs rely on scriptures such as the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, and the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
The latter three pairs rely on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. They distinguish that the One Vehicle is identical to the inexhaustible, while the Three Vehicles are indeterminate.
Concluding, it says: "What has been analyzed above, within these affiliated scriptures, seeks to manifest the perfect penetration and..."
Exhausting the entire treasury of the Dharma, the teachings and meanings of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), [the Buddha] manifested the name "One Vehicle" within the context of expedient means (*upāya*).
This was spoken so that those now entering [the path] might easily attain understanding, and so forth. Furthermore, it is said: "The aforementioned Dharma-gate subsumes all the lower teachings;
it belongs immediately to the primary meaning of the higher division, while the gradual [teachings] follow from its secondary meaning," and so on, up to the words "and..."

The final teaching of the Three Vehicles consists of "quiescent illumination and illuminating quiescence," the True Suchness of the Single Mark, as well as the teachings of the Initial Vehicle gate where defilement and purity are immediately empty, and the teachings on the Truth of Suffering of the Small Vehicle that adheres to the Dharma of the ignorant. It is clearly understood that the *Lotus Sūtra* simultaneously reconciles the provisional and the real, including both the Small Vehicle and the Three Vehicles.
If this is so, why does Zhiyi’s *Xuanyiwen* (Profound Meaning) state that the *Lotus Sūtra* merely reconciles the past?

Because of this [principle of] expediency, it is said that all three are merely provisional pointers. Since the past was not actually obstructed by expedient means, they were not brought together then.
Now, to say that the ultimate reality is what is ultimately brought together—how does this contradict the Patriarch? Answer:

That [critique] refuted the Dharma Master Guangzhai of the Liang dynasty, who established a teaching of four vehicles based on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Therefore, he distinguished what was contradictory [to the true intent], and thus made these remarks. It is for this reason...
The Master regards the three carts at the gate as provisional and the equal bestowal at the crossroads as real;
he holds that only the preaching of the *Lotus Sūtra* is real, yet he fails to recognize that it suppresses other definitive sūtras such as the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

This is because in the past, regarding the Great [Vehicle], he did not distinguish between the provisional and the real, and thus incurred the fault of suppressing various true teachings. Now, in order to harmonize the intent of the teachings, it is not so.
Therefore, there are three major sections in this exposition of the meaning. First, it clarifies the intent behind the "convergence" (*hui*) and "non-convergence.

By employing the three carts at the gateway as skillful means (*upāya*), the three provisional [vehicles] from the past are all shown to lack substantial reality; this is precisely the meaning of convergence. Thus, the Commentary states:
"Because it converges the provisional of the past, it is said that all three are empty designations. As for not converging the reality of the past, the reality of the past has already..."

In the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras, the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*) is revealed and elucidated; therefore, the Commentary states: "In the past, the reality was not obstructed by the provisional means, and thus they were not brought together.
Second, the intent of "harmonizing the two" and "harmonizing the three" is clarified. The *Yanyi* (Exegesis of Meaning) explains: "Both approaches possess their own rationale.
To refute the Small Vehicle and reveal the Great Vehicle is 'harmonizing the two. To bring the provisional back to the real is 'harmonizing the three. Third...
The "Three Clarities" (三明) take up the intention of what was previously abandoned. The *Shu* (Commentary) states: "If the provisional is opened to reveal the real, then the three are one;

there is no separate 'one' apart from them. The *Chao* (Sub-commentary) explains this with two meanings: first, clarifying the convergence of the three into one; second, clarifying the convergence of the three back into one.
Regarding the first, the convergence of the three into one: it takes the three provisional [teachings] of the past, which lack inherent substance, and converges them into one.
The revelation of the principles, practices, and fruits of the Dharma all derive from the single reality; as these are all causes for Buddhahood, they are termed "taking up the past.

As for "discarding the past," this refers to discarding the three previous teachings, each of which followed different paths. Now, following this subsequent disclosure and discarding, one realizes that the three are identical to the one.
The mind gives rise to joy, and one knows for oneself that one will become a Buddha; thus, the true mark (dharmatā) is revealed. This is...
Therefore, the sub-commentary first cites the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter to prove that the practices of the Small Vehicle are themselves the cause of Buddhahood;

it next cites the "Chapter on Resolute Faith" to prove that the practices of the Great Vehicle are what they possess, even stating: "Now, this commentary seeks to reconcile these three causes into a single cause;
thus it cites both passages, both clarifying the reconciliation of practice. Hence it is said: 'Reconciling the three into one. Next...

Regarding "Clarifying the Unification of the Three into One," the *Shu* (Commentary) states: "If one sets aside the provisional to establish the real, they are explained as four in meaning, such as combining three dots to form the character 'I' (*ī*), and so forth.

The *Yanyi* (Exposition of Meaning) states: "If one sets aside [the provisional]... This clarifies that the three of the past are unified into the one of the present. Within this, there are two parts:
first, unifying the past to form the present, which consists of the principle (*dharma*), the analogy, and the application. Regarding the principle, it says: "They are explained as four in meaning."

Fourth: Because [the teaching] merely abolishes the former three teachings, asserting that "three are provisional while one is real," it reveals that outside of the three there is no separate dharma of the one reality.
Thus, it is said that there are four in terms of meaning, yet only three are distinct while the one is the totality.

This is like the metaphor of gathering the three dots below; this borrows from the second chapter of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* regarding the formation of the character "I" (*ī*) from the three dots, and so forth, even stating: [text continues].

Now, I borrow this analogy but do not adopt its underlying principle. That is to say, the three dots are used as a metaphor for the Three Vehicles, while their formation into the character *ī* serves as a metaphor for the One Vehicle.
When the Three Vehicles are explained separately, all three are provisional; when the three are combined into one, it is therefore called "real.
It is not that there is another dot outside of the three dots; rather, by combining them all into one, it is thus established.

Fourth. The subsequent commentary states: "If, according to the past, it was not explicitly taught that all possess the seeds of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, and now they are all said to be perfected, then there is a difference between the present and the past. Thus, the *Yanyi* (Exegesis) explains:
"From 'If, according to the past' onwards, the second [section] clarifies how the present differs from the past. Previously, the three were merely combined into one, with no distinct dharma."
The four vehicles have already been established; now, to distinguish the One Vehicle as having its own distinct dharma-gate makes these four meanings clearly manifest.
This is that which was not previously taught but is now taught for the first time. It is the hearing of what has never been heard before—the unprecedented Dharma.
That is to say, although the Great Vehicle previously existed and also taught the principles of the Tathāgatagarbha-nature, Nirvāṇa, and the Dharmakāya as being truly eternal, it had not yet...
The Buddha has clearly proclaimed that all sentient beings are endowed with the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision;
he appears in the world for this one purpose alone, and not for any other. Thus, Master Rui said: "As for the various Prajñā sūtras, there is no depth they do not reach to the utmost;
thus, those who seek the Way take them as their refuge. There is no greatness they do not encompass; thus, those who ride upon the vehicle [take them as their path]."
Yet, in their general outline, they all take "adapting to transformation" as their foundation. Regarding the gate of exhortation, one cannot help but employ skillful means (*upāya*).
Although the awakening of beings through these means and transformations is vast, they do not definitively establish the ultimate reality;

rather, they all pertain to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. This is indeed appropriate. The three points above harmonize and clarify the essential purport of the teachings of the *Lotus Sūtra*. This is the general meaning.

This merely clarifies that the three [vehicles] are unified into one. However, because there are two stages—initial and final—in the unification of capacities, the initial stage establishes the principle of unifying the past to achieve the present;

this is the first gate of skillful means. Unifying the provisional to return to the real is termed "unifying the three into one. This is explained as the four vehicles to manifest the harmonious integration of the three and the one;
it is identical to this meaning of Qingliang (Chengguan). This is precisely as stated in the second section of the *Jiaozhang* (Treatise on the Teachings).

In the section on "Clarifying the Inclusion and Benefit," it says: "If one first causes them to attain liberation through the three vehicles, and subsequently employs skillful means to lead them to the One Vehicle, this is a teaching that harmonizes the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles; therefore, it belongs to the category of 'Teaching in Common' (*tongjiao*). It continues:

"...including the inclusion of sentient beings to achieve the two benefits," and so forth. Furthermore, in the seventh gate of the subsequent "Selection" (*zhe*), it says: "There may be some sentient beings..."

Born into this world, those whose faculties regarding the Three Vehicles are indeterminate and who are capable of entering the Sameness Teaching of the One Vehicle perceive that all the dharmas of the Three Vehicles they have attained arise based upon the inexhaustible teaching of the One Vehicle;
these are its skillful means and provisional designations (*āgama-prajñapti*). Therefore, whatever they cultivate, they dedicate it all toward the One Vehicle, as in the assembly.

"The three refuges and so forth—this is the interpretation of Xianxiu (Wǒng-hyǒ). Furthermore, as in Zhìxiàng (Jisang), who horizontally relies on the provisional [teachings], his second point states:
'The One Vehicle is taught as a provisional means for that ultimate, perfect One Vehicle;

it is not itself the perfectly pervasive and sovereign [truth]. This is the interpretation of the Fourth Patriarch. Next is established the principle of clarifying how the present differs from the past. Thus it concludes, followed by the demonstration.
The true aspect [is revealed by] bestowing the great vehicle upon the open ground; this manifests only the One Vehicle and is not for others.
This is the meaning of "coolness" (*śītalatva*). Furthermore, as stated in the eighth section of the *Viniścaya*:

"There may be sentient beings who, within this world, because their faculties for the three vehicles are indeterminate, are capable of entering the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle; one should know that those [faculties] are the three vehicles."

These dharmas are fundamentally non-different. As for the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), why is this? It is because it serves as the designation for them, and there is no further distinct entity.

The conclusion of the Chapter on Determination states: This process of decline and flourishing reveals the relative heights and depths, as well as the increase and decrease, of the stages; thus, the general principle can be understood.

This principle applies to both that which is produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-ja*) and that which is innate (*prakṛti-stha*). It is not something known by those of the three vehicles or the Lesser Vehicle.
The Universal Worthy’s Nature-Arising (*Samantabhadra-prakṛti-utpāda*) resides within this stage. Why is this? Because it is the same realization. Zhizhang further stated:

"As the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* explains, the six definitive meanings constitute the essence (*tattva*) of these stages; they do not, conversely, rely on the number ten to designate them as the 'Ten Stages' (*daśabhūmi*).
Their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), however, are designated by employing the number ten. By examining and seeking through this, one comes to know [it]."

The Buddha’s compassion desires to make [the teaching] easy to understand; thus, he employs the characteristics of a complete enumeration of doctrinal categories to represent the essence of an incomplete enumeration of doctrinal categories—this is the Buddha’s special intention.
△ Third, clarifying the skillful means of the scripture’s core doctrine.
The Chapter states: "The scriptural text is skillful, interweaving two meanings to clarify the boundaries of the doctrine;
it is most excellent and sublime. The Commentary explains: This comprehensively reveals the dharma-gates of the eight assemblies of this single sutra.

By relying on the three to manifest the one, the preceding and succeeding sections are interwoven, skillfully gathering in those with various capacities to elucidate the ultimate boundaries of the profound and wondrous principle of the One Vehicle—both Perfect and Distinct. Thus, the two meanings are interwoven.

As for "meaning" (*artha*): it refers to the interweaving of the meanings of the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles. It also refers to the interweaving of the two meanings of the essence of the stages (*bhūmi*) and the characteristics of the stages.
Furthermore, Qingliang said: Regarding the three points of essential purpose (*tātparya*), there is first the general and then the specific. The general has two meanings:

first, taking the cultivation of practice through the stages—by means of wisdom, abandonment, and realization—as the essential purpose, in order to manifest the aspect of practice that is perfectly interfused and unimpeded.

"Destination. Both of the preceding two are the "thesis" (*zong*); they serve as the destination for the fruit of Buddhahood. This clarifies the interweaving of the two meanings of "thesis" (*zong*) and "destination" (*qu*).
Regarding the subsequent "particularity": it is distinct from the preceding "generality," and briefly comprises ten points. Even unto the tenth, it says:
"Tenth is the 'synopsis,' meaning that the six determinations are discerned through this thesis. It further states: "If one examines its essential nature (*tixing*), for the most part it is not..."

The preceding [categories] are presented; for the sake of completing the number ten, there are slight additions and subtractions. The first is the essence that transcends words; the second is the essence of what is realized;

and so on, up to the tenth, which is the essence of the cause alone. These are taken according to their distinct characteristics, as they differ from the ocean of fruits. These ten essences are thus subsumed.
These do not exceed three aspects: first, the aspect of total inclusion; second, the aspect of specific realization, which refers to the arising of wisdom and the manifestation of realization;
and third, the ineffable aspect, the correspondence of which can be understood. The former two are the cause, and the latter one is the fruit. Cause and fruit are neither identical nor separate;
as both speech and thought are transcended, this constitutes the essence of the ground (*bhūmi*). The three sections above are subsumed within the sixth question-and-answer discussion.

The sixth section clarifies the essential nature of the six determinations. Together with the preceding five categories, this concludes the fifth section, which elucidates the dharma-gate of the one sūtra across eight assemblies.
△ Next, the sixth section clarifies the differences in the three types of *tri-samaya* dependent origination; the text is further divided into three parts.
The third section, "The Pure Dependent Origination of the Three Vehicles," states:
"The dependent origination of the three vehicles is such that when conditions aggregate, there is existence; when conditions disperse, there is separation.

The commentary explains: There are two types of dependent origination: first, the defiled, and second, the pure. The defiled refers to sentient beings of the six realms who are deluded regarding the Truth.

**Grasping at the False:** Internally, one gives rise to a deluded mind; externally, one clings to deluded objects. When these two conditions—mind and object—interact through falsehood, defilement arises.

Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "Ignorance perfumes True Suchness, giving rise to all defiled dharmas. **The Pure:** This refers to those of the provisional and gradual capacities of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
Knowing that defilement constitutes a fault, they seek purity by departing from the true nature. This is precisely the Three Vehicles: first, the Śrāvaka.

1. The Vehicle of the Listeners (*śrāvakayāna*): This involves practicing the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-viṣaya-sthāpana-bhāvanā*) and the seven stages of expedient means (*sapta-saṃbhāra*). 2. The Vehicle of the Solitary Realizers (*pratyekabuddhayāna*): This involves awakening to the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) and becoming a *pratyekabuddha*.
Because these two vehicles eliminate only the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) but have not yet eliminated the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), they are said to be "partially purified.

3. The Vehicle of the Bodhisattvas: Having heard the teachings on the five natures and the three vehicles, one believes in the principle of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*) and does not grasp [at phenomena].
In my teaching, although one may give rise to the three minds and four vows, this is merely a wearying of provisional conditioned phenomena and a longing for Bodhi;

it still falls into the duality of grasping and rejecting. Although one may cultivate the six perfections and myriad practices, sever the two obstacles, and realize the two emptinesses, these are the True Suchness manifested by the two emptinesses, rather than the two emptinesses being identical to True Suchness itself. In meaning, this corresponds to the stage of the provisional beginning.

This is purity. Although the Sudden and Gradual Teachings recognize the true nature (*tathatā*) as being without distinct eight consciousnesses, they remain constrained by the process of overturning and merging;
thus, they first eliminate faults and only later establish virtues. Therefore, when pure dependent origination arises, it is provisionally gathered as existence;

when pure conditions disperse, the illusion ceases as separation. These states of gathering, dispersing, and separating do not accord with the nature (*dharmatā*). This is [the nature of] dependent origination.
At this juncture, it is fundamentally ultimate and free from the act of cultivation; therefore, it is called "purity within its own sphere" (*bun-jō*).

This progressive "purity within its own sphere" reveals that the preceding four teachings are all pure within their respective spheres and all belong to the Three Vehicles, serving as the objects of contrast.
This is explained in detail in the *Gyōgan-gi-ki* (Record on the Meaning of the Vows). Even if the final, sudden, and perfect [teachings] were combined as three...
Although it is ultimately and suddenly real, its provisional aspects are not yet sufficient; therefore, it does not distinguish the perfect fusion of all virtues.

Thus, Xianshou said: "Though there are differences between the sudden, the gradual, and the three types of provisional and real teachings from beginning to end, they are collectively categorized as the teaching of the Three Vehicles, because they are all attained by the three types of persons," and so forth.
Furthermore, following the section on the Ten Mysterious Gates of Dependent Origination, he distinguishes them, saying: "This is..."
Therefore, the Great Sage is skillful; within the stages of those three vehicles, he provisionally teaches little according to their capacities and inclinations.

Because they do not exhaustively fathom the source of the Dharma-realm, he manifests provisional two-body and three-body Buddhas, yet does not reveal the self-boundary of the ten bodies of all Buddhas.
Hence, it is called the "pure-part dependent origination. △ Second, the Perfect Purity of the One Vehicle.

On Dependent Origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). The chapter states: "The dependent origination of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*): when conditions gather, there is nothing that exists; when conditions disperse, there is nothing from which one is separated. The commentary explains:

The essential body (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle is entirely dependent origination based on nature (*xing*). This nature pervades the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and thus dependent origination is boundless. When [conditions] gather...

When it manifests as wondrous existence, that existence is not permanent; therefore, it is said to be "not existent. When it disperses into true emptiness, that emptiness is not a state of annihilation;

therefore, it is said to be "not departed from. It is like a bright mirror: when reflecting a gathering of forms, it does not retain them; when reflecting their dispersion, its nature is fundamentally not separate from them. Zhixiang said:

"In elucidating the single vehicle’s dharma-realm of dependent origination, one reaches the ultimate limit of both the fundamental and the derivative, remaining free from artificial cultivation and fabrication."
Why is this? Because it is free from marks (*lakṣaṇa*). To "arise" means to arise within the great understanding and great practice;

within the bodhicitta that is free from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), this is called "arising. Because it is of the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it is said to "arise.

Arising is non-arising; this non-arising is the arising of the nature (*dharmatā-udaya*). Xianshou said: "Because it is dependent origination, it is the true virtue of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*)."
The realm of Samantabhadra is characterized by the possession of virtue, sovereignty, and non-obstruction. As the *Avataṃsaka* states:
"The Bodhisattva skillfully contemplates the dharma of dependent origination; within a single dharma, they understand manifold dharmas, and within manifold dharmas, they understand a single dharma."
Therefore, one should know that within the one there are ten, and within the ten there is the one; they interpenetrate without obstruction, yet they do not become identical with one another.

This is likewise true for all other categories. Thus, in the perfectly pure dependent origination, the principles and meanings of each door are such that every phenomenon arises through conditions, and each is inexhaustible.
It encompasses both emptiness and existence while transcending all marks; it enters into words and images yet leaves no trace. This is explained at length in the sixth and seventh [chapters].

The *Zuxingyuan Chao* (Commentary on the Patriarch’s Vows) explains this in full detail; it need not be recorded here at length. △ Third, the conclusion clarifying that the intermingled manifestations reveal the Perfect.
The chapter states: "This is because the objects they correspond to are different; thus, they form an intermingled manifestation to clarify [the truth]."

The commentary states: The preceding section clarifies "partial purity" (*vibhāga-śuddhi*) as a contrast to the "perfect purity" (*pariśuddhi*) of the *Pratītyasamutpāda-dharmaparyāya*, which is like clouds rising in the vast sky;
its myriad practices are in full bloom, comparable to flowers opening upon brocade. Thus, Master Xianshou distinguished it, saying:
"It is entirely different and distinct from that of the Three Vehicles. One should extensively rely upon the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* as the universal object of the Universal Eye (*samantacakṣus*).
Realm. Reflect upon this accordingly. The above three sections conclude the sixth [part], the differentiations of the single causal origination (*ekāśraya-pratītyasamutpāda*).

Next, the seventh [section] shall clarify the mutual support of cause and effect within the same substance (*samavāyin*). This text is further divided into two parts. First, the equality based on the substance.
The chapter states: Furthermore, it is like a single substance serving as both support and basis to clarify cause and effect. The essence of the rational nature is harmoniously integrated;
when in the state of cause, it acts as cause, and when in the state of fruit, it acts as fruit. Its nature is equal, yet it is explained according to conditions.

The commentary states: The single principle-body of the Dharma-realm is equal like empty space; it serves as the substratum for both the holy and the ordinary, and functions as the support for both the holy and the ordinary.

Although there are differences in capacity and distinctions between cause and effect regarding its functioning and the cultivation toward the realization of the unconditioned (*asamskṛta*), the single rational nature is nonetheless equal, harmonious, and integrated. Therefore, from the perspective of the gate of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)...

Within this, the two gates of identical substance and different substance are inexhaustible. Thus, Xianshou said: "The first gate of identical substance already encompasses both the gates of identical and different substance.
Inexhaustibility within inexhaustibility enumerates ten forms of inexhaustibility; exhausting their perfect culmination, there is nothing in the Dharma-realm that is not subsumed.
Therefore it is said: "In the state of cause, it is the cause; in the state of fruition, it is the fruition; its nature is equal."
This is explained according to the conditions [of the audience]. △ Second, the differentiation according to conditions. The chapter states:
"In the One Vehicle, it is perfectly luminous and endowed with all virtues; in the Three Vehicles, it is a solitary gate of a single aspect.

In the Small Vehicle, the profound is discarded and the shallow is discussed; among ordinary beings, there is only the empty text of phenomena. This is precisely the wondrous intent of the Principle."
The commentary states: The *Shizhuan Xuanzhang* (Ten Profound Chapters on the Ultimate Characteristics) says: "In the One Vehicle, there is immediate, perfect enlightenment endowed with all virtues.

This means that this One Vehicle encompasses the ocean of the fruit within its causal stage, and the source of the cause is reached through its fruition; it is a perfectly pure dependent origination, possessing infinite virtues. Master Xianshou said:

The Sūtra states, "At the very moment of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, one immediately attains perfect awakening, fully endowed with the body of wisdom, without depending on others for realization."
Thus, there are immeasurable such [passages], as detailed in the sūtra. Even to the point where it is asked: "These merely praise the virtues within the cause;

how can they be the fruition of perfected virtue? The answer to this single point is that cause and effect are of one essence (*ekātman*), forming a single dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
By attaining this, one attains that, because this and that are mutually identical. If the fruit were not attained, then the cause...
This does not constitute a valid cause. Why? Because that which fails to produce a fruit is not a cause. Furthermore, it is said:
"Since the essence of this cause is established in dependence upon the fruit, when the cause is fulfilled, it simply vanishes into the ocean of the fruit.

Because this serves as proof for the realm of realization, it cannot be described in words. Next, it says: "Abiding within the Three Vehicles, one encounters the solitary gate of the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*)."

Worthy One, the Commentary explains: The three vehicles merely accord with the capacities of beings; they do not yet manifest the self-boundary of the ten bodies of the Buddhas, and thus do not manifest the Buddha-body.
Furthermore, they provide only brief teachings according to capacity—such as the single characteristic, the single quiescence, and the single flavor of principle—which are not exhaustive teachings.
Why is this? Because for the three vehicles, such [exhaustiveness] would constitute a fault.
And so forth. Next, it says: "Regarding those in the Hīnayāna who discard the profound and discuss only the shallow":

this refers to how, within the extremely profound dependent origination of the single-mind dharma, they rely on the shallow wisdom of the *saviṣaya-vijñāna* (consciousness of objective phenomena) to contemplate the formations of dependent origination, rather than relying on the profound wisdom of the *karma-vijñāna* (consciousness of karmic activity).

One may obtain its name but not yet comprehend its meaning. For example, as the Śrāvaka treatises state, there are only six consciousnesses, which are conceptually divided into *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna*.
Furthermore, as the *Ekottarika Āgama* states regarding the *ālayavijñāna*, one merely obtains its name.
Therefore, the "Chapter on Dependent Origination" by Zhizhi (Zhìxiàng) says: "If categorized by superiority and inferiority, dependent origination is the superior contemplation; it is also..."

Regarding the One Vehicle: although its name exists within the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), its meaning is not realized therein. Why is this? Because the dharma-self (dharma-ātman) has not been severed.
Next, it says: "Those who abide in the mundane realms and merely engage with the literal text of emptiness" refers to the six classes of ordinary beings.

Deluded emotions obscure wisdom. Although one may achieve success through the practice of dependent origination, the ten wholesome paths, and the five precepts—resulting in a rebirth that transcends the realms of desire and form—one remains bound by the meditations on phenomena (*dhyāna*) and does not penetrate the contemplation of principle (*tattva*). Therefore, it is said that these are "merely matters of empty texts.

Thus, the *Yuanqi Zhang* (Chapter on Dependent Origination) by Zhizhi states: "Dependent origination is that which the Great Sage employs to gather sentient beings, desiring to lead them to accord with principle and abandon phenomena. Ordinary people..."
To perceive phenomena is to be deluded regarding principle; the Sage attains principle precisely within phenomena. The four lines above describe differences based on conditions;
although there are distinctions in depth from the Sage down to the ordinary person, they all in fact manifest principle. Thus, phenomena and principle are fused and identical.
Thus, the great dependent origination is established. Therefore, the conclusion states: "This is precisely the subtle essence of principle. Consequently, Zhizang further says:
"Now, by citing the true principle to harmonize with deluded sentiments, I cause all sentient beings to know that phenomena are themselves non-existent, and to realize principle through phenomena;
for this reason, this teaching is promulgated. The two preceding sections are subsumed under the seventh [section], which clarifies the cause of identical substance (*tongti-yin*).

The "Fruit as the Support" (Phala-āśraya), together with the preceding [sections], constitutes seven categories in total, all of which are subsumed within the initial introduction. This concludes the section on the "Explanation of the Causes and Conditions.

Now follows the second part: the "Correct Exposition of the Common and Distinct [Teachings]. This section is divided into ten parts. First is the "Wisdom of the Common and Distinct Dharmas," which provides inexhaustible benefit for those of sharp faculties.
The text is further divided into two parts. The first concerns the inexhaustibility of the causes and effects of the specific teachings of the One Vehicle.
The chapter states: "Furthermore, the Dharma of the One Vehicle is distinguished according to the capacities of sentient beings; it is not that its own characteristics are distinct.

It is spoken of as having distinct characteristics in accordance with those capacities, and each of these distinctions possesses ten aspects. The reason for speaking of ten is to manifest their immeasurability."

The commentary states: The distinct teachings of the One Vehicle clarify ten categories of dharma-meaning—such as teaching, principle, cause, fruit, phenomenon, noumenon, virtue, and function—each of which is uniquely distinct and constitutes the great boundary of the dharmadhātu dependent origination, encompassing all phenomena without exception.

If one refers to the ultimate realization of the fruit, it does not depend on the capacity of the recipient; because the ocean of fruition transcends language, its characteristics cannot be described.

This is the distinction of their characteristics; therefore, it is said that they are not distinguished by means of their own individual marks (*svalakṣaṇa*). Now, we clarify the realm of Samantabhadra:

through universal causes and universal dharmas, there is universal benefit for all capacities (*yogya*), such that both capacity and dharma are universal. Each and every one possesses the ten [perfections], and each of these ten is inexhaustible, thereby manifesting the infinite.
Thus, Master Xianshou said: "The dependent origination of the Dharma-realm extends even to the state of non-existence..."
Exhaustive. Now, for the sake of brevity, these essential gateways are summarized into two. First is the meaning of the realization of the ultimate fruit, which is the self-realm of the ten Buddhas.
Second is the meaning of the teachings distinguished according to causes in accordance with conditions, which is the realm of Samantabhadra.
Regarding the first meaning: it is perfectly interfused and sovereign; the one is all, and all is one. It is ineffable.
This is merely its formal appearance. It continues until it says: "Whether it be Indra or something subtle, none are excluded. Thus, the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) states:
"The causal aspect can be described; the resultant aspect cannot be described. This refers precisely to that matter.

Therefore, the present text, by means of the cause in relation to the capacities of sentient beings, reveals the distinct dharma of the One Vehicle, which is equally possessed by both the holy and the ordinary, fully embodying the single essence from the very beginning.
It is immeasurable. Therefore it is said: because one wishes to manifest the immeasurable, the principal and its attendants are perfectly interfused, such that each and every one is immeasurable.
Master Hui’s commentary states: "To be 'extraordinary and independent' and name it 'distinctive' misses the mark regarding its own characteristics.
This openly contradicts the Patriarchal Explanations. [This concludes] the evaluation at the end of the fascicle. 2. The Single Vehicle shares the same Dharma-wisdom as the inexhaustible.

The chapter states: Furthermore, regarding the single vehicle (ekayāna) as a commonality of dharma, its identity is manifested in contrast to wisdom. If one draws in the capacities [of sentient beings] to realize this identity, then the identities within identities possess ten aspects, which exhaustively reach the inexhaustible.

The commentary states: Regarding the harmonious and interfused Dharma of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), there are two gates concerning the qualities and functions of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*):

first, the gate of distinct entities; second, the gate of identical entities. Furthermore, within the initial gate of distinct entities, there are two parts: first, the mutual identity of emptiness and existence based on the two meanings of self and other, which are said to be identical from the perspective of their essence.
First, when the One Vehicle itself possesses its own essence, the infinite vehicles of others— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available content.*
It must be because there is no [separate] cause. Therefore, the self is identical to the other. Why? Because the self has no function apart from that which is produced by the other.
Thus the Patriarch said: "Because the two exist and the two are empty, each does not coexist; since they do not coexist, they are not non-identical.

Because existence and non-existence are neither existent nor non-existent, they are non-dual. Therefore, the One Vehicle is identical to the infinite vehicles, for they are constantly mutually identical. Thus it is.
The Patriarch said: "If it were not so, the principle of dependent origination would not be established, as there would be the fault of [things] having intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and so forth.
Next, regarding the two meanings of power and lack of power—whether from one's own side or from another—their function is said to be the same.

Because the One Vehicle possesses its own full power, it is able to encompass the immeasurable vehicles of others; because those many other vehicles possess no power at all, they are able to enter [into it].
This is self-evident. The principle that "others have power while one lacks it" can be understood by reversing the above.

Thus, Xianshou said: "When the function subsumes the essence, there is no separate essence; therefore, they are merely mutually inclusive (*xiangru*). When the essence subsumes the function, there is no separate function;

therefore, they are merely mutually identical (*xiangji*). Furthermore, he asked: "Regarding the aforementioned gateways of meaning concerning the 'one' and the 'many,' do they coincide simultaneously?"
"Is it that the preceding and succeeding are different? Answer: "They are identical, yet they are both preceding and succeeding. Why is this?
Because this Dharma-nature of dependent origination is complete; its counter-flow and forward-flow are of one essence, not contradicting its virtuous functions, and it is sovereign and unobstructed."
Therefore, the second gate, the Gate of Identical Substance (*sābhāva-dvāra*), encompasses the many within the one and the one within the many; the one is the many, and the many is the one.

This is entirely consistent with and exhaustively subsumes the two preceding gates of distinct substance (*nānābhāva-dvāra*). Thus, Master Xianshou said: "The gate of identical substance subsumes both the gates of identity and difference;
it is inexhaustible and inexhaustible, reaching the ultimate perfection of the *dharmadhātu*. There is nothing that is not fully contained therein.
This does not exhaustively encompass [the meaning]. The Patriarch asked again: "What is the difference between this and the previous case of 'different substances'? He replied:

"Regarding the previous case of different substances, the first [substance] is viewed in contrast to the subsequent nine; they enter one another through different gates (*dvāra*). Now, in this case of identical substance, the ten are inherently complete within the single [substance];

it is not spoken of as entering through different gates by being viewed in contrast to what precedes or follows. This principle should also be applied accordingly when considering the meaning. Thus we know that, because there is no obstruction...
Non-obstruction of wisdom refers to the wisdom that accords with reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*) and the wisdom that accords with phenomena (*yathāmātra-jñāna*).
Thus, even the three wisdoms and four wisdoms are all without obstruction, thereby achieving a profound and inexhaustible interpenetration. This is because wisdom is unobstructed:
one wisdom is all wisdoms. Because objects are unobstructed: one object is all objects. Thus, object and wisdom each possess the non-obstruction of the one and the many, in mutual correspondence.
Therefore, Master Xianshou said: "If one were to discard wisdom (*jñāna*), one would not discuss dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

It is because of the perspective of wisdom that it is said to have been thus from the beginning. Why? Because if it were unestablished, that would be the end of it; but once established, it is free from beginning and end.
Since wisdom arises, the Dharma has been established from the outset. Question: Is this due to wisdom, or is the nature of the Dharma itself such? Answer: It is due to wisdom.
Such is the nature of the Dharma. Why is this? Because they are simultaneously and fully present. Therefore, it is said that the correspondence with the sense organs manifests their identity.
By means of the unobstructed realm of the *dharmadhātu* in correspondence with unobstructed wisdom, the inconceivable, perfect, and pervasive identity of the Great Dependent Origination is revealed.
If one considers the guidance of sentient beings according to their capacities, the essence and its virtues are both universal and particular, yet their convergence and identity are inexhaustible.

Therefore, it is said that the "identical identity" possesses the ten inexhaustibles. For this reason, the Dharma of the One Vehicle universally encompasses both the holy and the ordinary through the dedication of wisdom;

it harmonizes and merges them into non-duality, being one with the single *dharmadhātu*. Thus, Xianshou, following and upholding [this tradition], specifically composed his *Jiaozhang* (Treatise on the Teachings), stating:
"Regarding the two types of identical teaching: first, the various vehicles are differentiated; later, the root and the branches are harmonized. It continues: "This..."

The teaching of the same vehicle (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*) explains that all vehicles are harmonized and fused into non-duality, being one within the single *dharmadhātu*. It even states: "The One Vehicle is precisely the Three;

though they possess both concealment and manifestation, they are ultimately and eternally inexhaustible. This clearly shows that establishing the general name "same" is to manifest the *Ekayāna* of the *Avataṃsaka*, which directly clarifies the *dharmadhātu*.
Because its principle is universally pervasive, it is in its entirety non-dual. This is not the same as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, which [teaches] horizontally...

Relying on skillful means, he refutes difference to reveal unity. [The claim that] Master [Zhiyi] established the Lotus Assembly to harmonize the three vehicles into one, thereby collectively subsuming all those who share the same [nature], is an error;

this shall be critiqued at the end of the scroll. The above two sections conclude the first part, clarifying how the wisdom of the Dharma benefits sentient beings through both common and distinct capacities without end. △ Second, examining the common and distinct paths of realization.

The distinctions in their characteristics are discussed; the text further divides into four parts. First, regarding the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), it is argued that its discourse on the Path is necessarily contentious.
The chapter states: "Furthermore, because the Small Vehicle has not exhausted its discourse on the Path, its arguments are contentious."

The commentary states: The preceding section on the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra concerns the ultimate One Vehicle, the fundamental nature of phenomena—both their commonality and their distinctions—which all Buddhas and sentient beings equally possess.
Nevertheless, due to differences in the capacities of beings and the diversity of the teachings, [the path is presented in various ways].
The Way has its great aspects and its small aspects. [The former] establishes faith through the reality of ultimate principle and the skillful means [of the latter].
Yet, being unable to exhaustively investigate the One True Great Way, they compete to divide their own schools.

This is what is meant by the term "sectarian treatise" (*zonglun*). Thus, Zhizang said: "If within the Small Vehicle there were only [the teachings of] the Śrāvakas, it would constitute the school of the Small Vehicle; it is not [otherwise]."
Because they have attained the emptiness of dharmas, because they have not exhausted the source of dharmas, and because their teaching is incomplete, there are many disputes and arguments.
△ Second, regarding the two vehicles and... [text missing].
The chapter states: "Regarding the Three Vehicles and the Shared Teaching, when one exhaustively investigates their discourse on the Way, there is a definitive conclusion.

The commentary explains: "[... because the Sudden Teaching explicates reality, it alone attains the gate of True Suchness (tathatā) wherein both subject and object are extinguished. The discourse on the Way is thus determined; this extinction transcends verbal expression."
Therefore, Xianshou said: "In the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao), there are three [aspects]: the beginning and the end are both transcended. Next, the Final Teaching (Zhong-jiao) also elucidates reality;

it only attains the Gate of True Suchness (Tathatā-mukha) wherein subject and object both exist. It discusses the certainty of the Way because it exhausts the principles of phenomena, rendering verbal discourse unnecessary.

All are attained by three types of persons; thus, they are collectively categorized as the three vehicles (*triyāna*). Nevertheless, there is a distinction between the sudden and the gradual.

The three vehicles of the sudden teaching are entirely detached from both beginning and end, constituting a single teaching in themselves. The three vehicles of the gradual teaching, however, differentiate between the beginning and the end.
Therefore, the Patriarch said: "The three delusions are opened into three [teachings], meaning that within them are differentiated the two teachings of the beginning and the end.
These are precisely those mentioned above in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* and other texts; among the three wheels of the Dharma, these refer to the latter two.

Thus, we know that the Patriarch categorized the teachings according to the vehicles of the Dharma (*dharma-yāna*), and therefore pointed to the latter two wheels of the Dharma in the *Saṃdhinirmocana* as comprehensively encompassing both the beginning and the end. The Patriarch himself concluded:

It is said: "This is merely a classification of the teachings according to the phenomena (*dharma*). If one proceeds according to the meaning (*artha*) of the phenomena, it shall be distinguished separately below.

This 'separate distinction' refers to the differentiations explained below, as well as what is analyzed in the ninth section of the *Tanyuan* (Exploring the Profundity) under the heading 'Classifying the Teachings by Meaning.

Thus we know that when based on phenomena, the inclusion is universal; when based on meaning, the judgment is specific. Therefore, the *Yanyi* states: "Phenomena refer to their own substance; meaning is..."

This is because "Dharma" (the phenomenon) is general while "meaning" (its significance) is specific. Based on this, one can know that "Dharma" serves as the general category for subsumption, whereas "meaning" provides the basis for specific distinctions.

Thus, we know that when Xianshou first composed the *Jiaozhang* (Chapter on the Teachings), he relied on the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, wherein the essence of Dharma is broad and pervasive, subsuming the entirety from beginning to end.

Later, in the *Tanyuan* (Exploring the Profundities), he relied on the principles of the *lakṣaṇa* school (the School of Characteristics), wherein the meaning is restricted; he set forth the specific reasons for these distinctions, as the tenets and interpretations differ according to the respective schools.

This refers only to the Initial Teaching (Shijiao). Furthermore, Master [Zongmi] did not thoroughly investigate the intent of the Patriarch; his classifications and integrations based on dharma and meaning were distinct from [Xianshou’s].
He even remarked to Xianshou: "When you first composed the *Jiaozhang*, you took the Dharma-characteristics (Faxiang) as the Second Period and the Third Period as the final one.

The Master was ignorant of the distinctions between the Separate and Perfect Teachings, lost the source of the fundamental principle, failed to clarify the relationship between the root and the branches, and confused the process of selection.

All is lost. The five samādhis merge the two [vehicles] into one; as they merge into one, the two vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are extinguished, leaving no third vehicle to be reconciled. Therefore, it is called the "One Vehicle of the Identical Teaching" (*tongjiao yisheng*).
